options.metric: Sum of reported pedestrians injured per calendar year, 2013–2025, in Brooklyn-labeled police-reported motor vehicle crashes
options.denominator: None; annual count, not a rate
options.reason: Injury counts show the annual reported nonfatal pedestrian burden in an intuitive way.
options.answer: Reported pedestrian injuries fell from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, about 22% lower, but have risen from the 2020 low of 1,781.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how the annual number of pedestrians reported injured changed: it sums number_of_pedestrians_injured among police-reported crashes whose borough matches Brooklyn after trimming and case normalization, grouping crashes by calendar year from 2013 through 2025. The count fell from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025, but rose from 1,781 in 2020; this is a defensible measure of recorded injury burden, with no denominator and therefore no exposure-adjusted rate. It cannot establish whether risk per pedestrian trip improved or describe road safety beyond the reported crash-injury count. The check found zero missing injury fields in the 2013–2025 Brooklyn rows, so none were dropped for that reason; the plan excludes 9,700 Brooklyn crashes in partial 2026 and cannot assign 668,406 2013-onward crashes with NULL borough to Brooklyn, and year-boundary dates do not prove uninterrupted reporting.

options.metric: Sum of reported pedestrians killed per calendar year, 2013–2025, in Brooklyn-labeled police-reported motor vehicle crashes
options.denominator: None; annual count, not a rate
options.reason: Pedestrian deaths are the most severe outcome and may give a different picture from injury totals.
options.answer: Reported pedestrian deaths were 30 in 2013 and 39 in 2025, an increase of 9, with substantial year-to-year fluctuation.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the annual fatal pedestrian burden changed: it sums number_of_pedestrians_killed among police-reported crashes whose borough matches Brooklyn after trimming and case normalization, grouped by calendar year from 2013 through 2025. Deaths increased from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025, although the series fluctuates substantially (including 17 in 2020); this is a defensible severity-focused count, with no denominator and therefore no exposure-adjusted rate. It cannot establish whether fatality risk per pedestrian trip improved or describe nonfatal injuries and other dimensions of road safety. The check found zero missing fatality fields in the 2013–2025 Brooklyn rows, so none were dropped for that reason; the plan excludes 9,700 Brooklyn crashes in partial 2026 and cannot assign 668,406 2013-onward crashes with NULL borough to Brooklyn, and year-boundary dates do not prove uninterrupted reporting.

options.metric: Count of Brooklyn-labeled crashes per calendar year with at least one reported pedestrian injured or killed, 2013–2025
options.denominator: None; annual crash-event count, not a rate
options.reason: Counting each crash once measures the frequency of crashes that harmed at least one pedestrian, rather than the number of people harmed.
options.answer: Crashes with at least one reported pedestrian injury or death fell from 3,498 in 2013 to 2,766 in 2025, about 21% lower, after rising from the 2020 low of 1,724.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how often a Brooklyn crash involved a pedestrian casualty: for each calendar year from 2013 through 2025, it counts a police-reported crash once when number_of_pedestrians_injured or number_of_pedestrians_killed is greater than zero, using a borough value matched to Brooklyn after trimming and case normalization. These crashes declined from 3,498 in 2013 to 2,766 in 2025 but rose from 1,724 in 2020; counting crash events once is defensible for event frequency, but it is not a count of people harmed and has no denominator or exposure-adjusted rate. It cannot establish risk per pedestrian trip or the severity of injuries within those crashes. The check found zero missing values in either pedestrian field in the 2013–2025 Brooklyn rows, so none were excluded for missing classification fields; crashes with no reported pedestrian injury or death do not meet this metric, 9,700 Brooklyn crashes in partial 2026 are excluded, and 668,406 2013-onward crashes with NULL borough cannot be assigned to Brooklyn; year-boundary dates do not prove uninterrupted reporting.
